https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c07l.text: Image source, Europa Press via Getty Images Image caption, Pedro SÃ¡nchez has been criticised for blaming trafficking gangs and social media for the crisis By Paul Kirby ,Â Europe digital editor Â and Â Guy Hedgecoe ,Â Madrid correspondent Published 3 September 2026, 09:14 BST Updated 1 hour ago Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has said no-one foresaw the influx of 72,000 migrants in the exclave of Ceuta, as pressure mounts over his handling of the crisis. "It's absurd to think that the government knew and did nothing," SÃ¡nchez told Spain's parliament on Thursday, hours after tens of thousands of people joined protests across the country backed by opposition parties. SÃ¡nchez also maintained there was no evidence Morocco was behind the mass crossing and there had been "close co-ordination" between the two countries. A Spanish police report has highlighted the "total permissiveness" of Moroccan security forces, although senior officials insist it does not point the finger at Rabat. Although most of the migrants have been sent back to Morocco, some 5,000 remain on the streets and beaches of Ceuta, on the North African coast, including as many as 1,400 children. There have been several reports that Spanish officials had been warned of a rise in sea arrivals over the border at Ceuta, following a Spanish court ruling that many migrants misunderstood to mean they would not be pushed back if they swam across. Opposition People's Party leader Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o accused the government of lying and a cover-up, and said the prime minister should resign. Spain's handling of the migrant influx angered some of its European partners, and Italy responded by imposing border restrictions on arrivals from Spain. The large turnout for the demonstrations in Madrid and other cities on Wednesday underlined the pressure SÃ¡nchez is under domestically too. The protests were ostensibly held to express support for the people of Ceuta, but as frequent anti-government chants have shown, they also reflected public anger at the ongoing crisis. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Tens of thousands of Spaniards took to the streets to mark Ceuta Day on Wednesday evening As Thursday's fierce debate in Congress showed, the situation in Ceuta has developed from a humanitarian and logistical crisis into a major political challenge for the Socialist leader. One of the issues SÃ¡nchez is having to explain is his government's bilateral relationship with Morocco. He has tried to walk a delicate line between defending his refusal to blame Morocco while reprimanding it for the sovereignty claims it has been making in recent weeks on both Ceuta and its fellow Spanish exclave of Melilla. SÃ¡nchez has been careful until now not to criticise Rabat and he said he would stick to "proven, verified facts", although he did complain of "unacceptable" statements by two Moroccan ministers about Ceuta and its sister city Melilla. The two cities have the EU's only land borders in North Africa and SÃ¡nchez told parliament: "Ceuta is not the border of Spain, it is Spain on the border [of Europe]." Protests in Spain against government's handling of Ceuta migrant crisis Published 13 hours ago Sexual assaults happening almost every day in Ceuta, prosecutors say Published 1 day ago Violence breaks out in Ceuta as migrant crisis continues Published 5 days ago Politicians to both his left and right point to what they say is Morocco's track record of using the border with Spain as leverage when it has a grievance. Many have interpreted the police report pointing to the role of Moroccan security forces in the July crossing as reinforcing this theory, although SÃ¡nchez maintained there was no solid evidence of government involvement. Responding to the police report, as well as reports before the influx, FeijÃ³o told MPs that it had "originated in Morocco, was consented to by Morocco and there are indications that Morocco co-ordinated it and the Government knew because it had been warned about it". Morocco has denied orchestrating or being involved in the mass crossing. SÃ¡nchez praised the response of Ceuta police who had chosen to "defend human life" when the influx took place, rather than defend the border. He also highlighted close co-operation with Moroccan authorities over the return of more than 90% of the migrants in the following 72 hours. He addressed the "difficult times" faced by the residents of Ceuta, as he explained the "complexity" of what had happened on 30 and 31 July. He spoke of an "episode in which numerous actors and interests converge", doubling down on his assertion that hoaxes and rumours spread by social media had sparked the crisis. He has already blamed trafficking gangs and angered Russia and Israel for highlighting social media linked to both countries along with "an international far-right movement". He told MPs that there was no evidence of state actors being involved but doubled down on his allegations of accounts linked to the two countries. Ceuta was "a humanitarian crisis and also an administrative challenge within the city itself", he added. https://weeklyblitz.net/2026/09/13/roman.text: Title : Europe’s diesel vulnerability is becoming a strategic problem An “Islamic America” vision raises questions about faith, constitutional rights and civic identity Building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability US keeps boasting about militarizing space 60 years after Outer Space Treaty Europe is pushing for greater autonomy in outer space The Russian drone warning that Italy and France say never happened A steady course for China-US relations: Cooperation, stability and shared responsibility Africa’s AI opportunity: Building a future of practical and inclusive innovation US allies should watch Washington’s European force review closely US charges tech executive and Russian national over alleged hidden ownership of digital forensics firm Home Featured Romania: Kronospan subsidiaries accused of hiding toxic emissions Sonjib Chandra Das Update Time : Sunday, September 13, 2026 Romanian prosecutors have accused two subsidiaries of global timber giant Kronospan of illegally releasing hazardous pollutants into populated areas and manipulating environmental monitoring data to conceal dangerous emissions. Romanian prosecutors have brought criminal charges against two subsidiaries of Austrian timber company Kronospan, accusing them of releasing hazardous chemicals above legal limits and deliberately falsifying environmental records to create the appearance of regulatory compliance. The case, which follows a two-year investigation, centers on allegations that Kronospan Trading and Kronochem repeatedly concealed excessive emissions of nitrogen oxides and formaldehyde between 2022 and 2023. Two employees responsible for environmental oversight have also been charged in connection with the alleged violations. According to prosecutors, pollution levels at the companies’ facilities reached as much as three times the legally permitted threshold. Authorities allege that the emissions included formaldehyde, a carcinogenic substance widely used in the production of wood-based panels, as well as nitrogen oxides, which can contribute to respiratory illness and other serious health problems. The allegations are particularly significant because Kronospan operates large-scale industrial facilities close to populated areas in Romania. The company is one of the world’s leading producers of wood-based panels, supplying materials used in furniture, construction and interior products across European markets. At the heart of the prosecution’s case is an alleged system designed to manipulate environmental monitoring results. Romanian investigators claim that company personnel did not simply overlook pollution spikes. Instead, they allegedly repeated measurements whenever monitoring systems produced unfavorable results, withholding readings that showed excessive emissions and submitting only results that fell within acceptable limits. “Only values favorable to the company were transmitted to state authorities, thus creating the appearance of compliance,” prosecutors said in a statement. If proven in court, the allegations would amount to more than isolated failures in environmental monitoring. They would suggest that the companies deliberately interfered with a system intended to protect residents from industrial pollution and provide government regulators with accurate information about potentially dangerous emissions. An expert report prepared as part of the investigation reportedly concluded that the unmonitored releases were sufficiently serious to pose a potential threat to human health. Prosecutors said the risks were particularly concerning for people living in urban neighborhoods located near the industrial facilities. The investigation escalated in 2023, when Romanian authorities raided Kronospan’s local headquarters. Investigators had reportedly identified discrepancies between the company’s reported emissions figures and other information available to authorities, prompting a deeper examination of the company’s environmental practices. The resulting investigation focused not only on the amount of pollution allegedly released but also on how environmental data was collected, processed and communicated to regulators. Environmental monitoring is a critical component of industrial regulation. Companies operating facilities that emit potentially hazardous substances are generally required to measure emissions and provide authorities with reliable information. Regulators depend on those measurements to determine whether industrial operations remain within legal limits and whether additional safeguards are required. The prosecution alleges that this regulatory mechanism was compromised in the Kronospan case. Kronospan, however, has rejected the accusations and maintained that its Romanian operations comply with environmental requirements. In a statement provided to the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, the company expressed confidence that it would ultimately be cleared by the courts. “Both companies operate using Best Available Techniques on all production lines and have invested over 80 million euros in de-pollution equipment,” Kronospan said. The company also disputed the implication that it lacks effective environmental controls, saying emissions are subject to continuous monitoring in its on-site laboratories. That defense is likely to become central to the proceedings. The company’s claim that it uses modern pollution-control technology and has invested tens of millions of euros in environmental equipment directly challenges the prosecution’s assertion that emissions were deliberately concealed. The case also raises broader questions about the effectiveness of environmental oversight in areas dominated by large industrial operators. When regulators depend heavily on data supplied by companies themselves, the integrity of that information becomes essential. Any deliberate manipulation can potentially undermine the entire enforcement system. For residents living near industrial plants, the consequences can be particularly serious. Pollutants such as formaldehyde and nitrogen oxides can affect air quality and pose health risks when exposure is prolonged or concentrations become excessive. The prosecution’s claim that pollution levels reached several times the legal threshold therefore gives the case implications beyond corporate compliance. Kronospan’s operations in Romania form part of a much larger European timber-processing business. The company processes substantial volumes of wood and manufactures products that are distributed throughout international markets. Its size and economic importance make the allegations especially sensitive, as industrial activity provides employment and investment while simultaneously creating environmental responsibilities. The Romanian court proceedings will now determine whether prosecutors can substantiate their allegations against the two subsidiaries and the employees involved. The indictment itself does not establish guilt, and the defendants remain entitled to challenge the evidence presented by the prosecution. The central question before the court will be whether the alleged pollution violations resulted from operational failures or whether, as prosecutors contend, employees intentionally manipulated environmental monitoring to conceal illegal emissions. The answer could have consequences extending beyond Kronospan. A finding that industrial emissions data was systematically falsified would underscore the importance of independent environmental monitoring and stronger verification mechanisms for companies operating high-risk industrial facilities. For now, Kronospan maintains that its facilities comply with environmental standards and that its substantial investments in pollution-control technology demonstrate its commitment to responsible production. Romanian prosecutors, meanwhile, argue that technology and investment are not enough if the information provided to regulators cannot be trusted. As the case moves into the courtroom, evidence concerning emission measurements, laboratory records, monitoring procedures and communications with authorities is expected to play a decisive role. The proceedings will ultimately determine whether Kronospan’s Romanian subsidiaries violated environmental laws-and whether the alleged manipulation of pollution data helped hide the true scale of emissions from the communities living nearby. Photograph: Ben Birchall/PA US military US bombers pulled from RAF Fairford base after suspected terror plot Aircraft leave Gloucestershire base to return to US following arrest of dual British-Iranian national in central London Dan Sabbagh , Marina Dunbar , Charlie Moloney Sun 4 Oct 2026 17.25 EDT Last modified on Sun 4 Oct 2026 21.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US Air Force has pulled its bombers from RAF Fairford following an investigation into an alleged planned terror attack at the base. The bombers were redeployed back to their home bases in the US, according to a Pentagon official who was not authorised to discuss sensitive military movements and spoke on Sunday on condition of anonymity. A Pentagon spokesperson said: “While ⁠operational security precluded us from confirming the movement of our ​assets and forces in ‌real time, we can acknowledge ‌now that all US bombers that were deployed to ‌RAF Fairford have redeployed to their home stations in the United States.” At least 10 B-1 bombers of 12 flew out of Fairford on Sunday, including some that arrived on rotation less than a week ago, underlining the haste of the departure and the apparent significance given by the US to the threat. There was no immediate comment from the UK Ministry of Defence, though the rapid pace of the withdrawal will heighten concerns in the area around the RAF base in Gloucestershire. According to reporting by US media, the withdrawal appears to be in response to fresh or renewed security concerns about safety on the base. A report in the New York Times said: “American officials on Sunday declined to specify the nature of the new information that prompted the rapid withdrawal of the Air Force bombers, some of which had just arrived in the past week as part of a normal rotation of forces. “One US official said the new information was part of the same threat warnings that surfaced three weeks ago, but specific details and a sense of urgency spiked in the past 24 hours, alarming commanders.” A dual British-Iranian national was arrested in central London last week on suspicion of plotting a terror attack, following a security incident at RAF Fairford in late September. In total, six people have been taken into custody and then released on bail during the investigation. Suspect in RAF Fairford case called police to report incident Read more British authorities have linked the incident to Tehran. Iran has denied involvement. RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160km) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East. Its use in recent months came after then prime minister Keir Starmer granted Washington permission to use British bases for “defensive” strikes against Tehran. The US military still maintains a sizeable presence in the Middle East. On Thursday, a US official said the recently deployed USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier as well as the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group – a group of ships that together carry more than 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines – were heading for the region. The official said the move could result in three carriers being in the region as early as the end of October. https://www.dw.com/en/russia-frees-jaile.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OUfc Putin and Witkoff met in St. Petersburg for their ninth in-person talks Image: Kristina Solovyova/TASS/picture alliance Advertisement Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the release of US captive Stephen Hubbard during talks with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday. Hubbard had been taken captive by Russian forces on charges of being a mercenary, which he denies. He was sentenced to seven years in prison at a closed trial in 2024. Putin said Hubbard was at the airport and Witkoff said he was now "going home to his family." US President Donald Trump later said that he had made the request directly to Putin during a phone call last week. "The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return — an unprecedented situation for Russia," Trump claimed in a post on his Truth Social platform. "There was no 'swap' necessary for this release." A Russian court convicted Stephen Hubbard of being a mercenary in 2024, which he denies Image: Moscow City Court press service/AFP However, in a follow-up post, Trump also claimed that "numerous people" had called him to apologize after they criticized him for suspending a new round of sanctions , which he said was a necessary concession. "If sanctions would have been placed, certainly those negotiations would have come to a complete and total halt," Trump's post said. Putin, Witkoff to discuss Ukraine peace deal The release of Hubbard was seen as a goodwill gesture to the Trump administreation as the two sides discuss a peace deal in Ukraine . "We've brought some papers. It's really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you'll read that at your leisure," Witkoff told Putin. Putin proposed that Witkoff discuss the restoration of bilateral ties between Washington and Moscow, and the possibility of trilateral talks with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing. The meeting — the ninth such talks between Witkoff and Putin —comes a day after Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Norway , which US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described as "positive." "He will now, armed with those ideas, be able to ‌go to St. Petersburg and share them with the Russian side, and ‌let's ​see if we can make some progress," he said ahead of the talks. Witkoff to return to Oslo Witkoff's meeting with Zelenskyy and other European leaders in Oslo has brought fresh momentum to peace efforts, more than 4 years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Ukrainian leader remained in Oslo on Wednesday where met with lawmakers in the Norwegian parliament. Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said that Witkoff planned to return to Oslo for further consultations after his trip to St. Petersburg. "I think we may have entered a phase now where the Russians are also looking for opportunities for diplomacy," he told Norway's public broadcaster NRK on Wednesday morning. Nevertheless, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow was willing to listen but that he didn't expect any "miracle." Trump on Tuesday reiterated that he wants Zelenskyy "to make a deal."
